entries.note: A portmanteau acronym of founder [[from:Ingvar Kamprad]], his family farm Elmtaryd and his hometown Agunnaryd; product names follow a system based on Scandinavian places.
Jess's term for this episode for brand names built from parts of several words, such as [[see:IKEA]] and [[see:LEGO]].
An IKEA toilet brush named after the beautiful Lake Bolmen, shown in a 2021 Swedish tourism campaign.
An IKEA plant spray dropped in English-speaking countries because the name sounded rude in English.
An IKEA workbench whose name, meaning speedy, sounds unfortunate in English.
An IKEA computer desk whose name sounds rude in English.
An IKEA product name meaning happy home that looks like 'lick him' to English speakers.
IKEA's famous bookcase, an exception to the place-name system, named after advertising manager [[from:Billy Liljedahl]], who wanted a proper bookcase just for books.
A horror novel by Grady Hendrix about a haunted [[see:IKEA]]-type store, recommended by Jess.
From Danish [[from:leg godt]], play well; named in 1934 by Ole Kirk Christiansen; Americans say Legos, Britons play Lego; coincidentally Latin [[see:lego (Latin)]].
A company teaching physics to kids with LEGO, named after the meaning of [[see:LEGO]].
Latin for I read, also interpretable as I assemble or I collect, a serendipitous coincidence with [[see:LEGO]].
The name of the first version of [[see:LEGO]] bricks in the late 1940s.
1930s bricks that early [[see:LEGO]] bricks competed with.
A meaningless foreign-sounding name made up by Reuben and Rose Mattus in the Bronx in 1959 to look Danish, umlaut included.
A phrase German businesses tack onto names, along with 24, when they can't think of a brand name.
From Adi Dassler, nickname of [[from:Adolf Dassler]], who wanted Adas but found it taken after splitting from brother Rudolf.
Rudolf Dassler's company name, from Rudolf Dassler, later changed to [[see:Puma]].
Replaced [[from:Ruda]], keeping its vowels and length; perhaps chosen because an early Ruda logo had a puma, a fast, internationally pronounceable animal.
From Albrecht Discounts; feuding brothers both kept the name, creating [[see:Aldi Nord]] and [[see:Aldi Süd]].
One brother's half of [[see:Aldi]], found in northern Germany including Berlin.
The other half of [[see:Aldi]], in southern Germany and also the Aldi found in the US and Britain.
German supermarket named from syllables of Revisionsverband der Westkauf-Genossenschaften, Auditing Association of Western Buying Cooperatives.
German supermarket from the initials E-D-K, as pronounced in German, of Einkaufsgenossenschaft der Kolonialwarenhändler, Purchasing Cooperative of Colonial Goods Retailers.
Berlin's most famous department store, short for Kaufhaus des Westens.
British supermarket from Associated Dairies, built the same uncreative way as German names like [[see:Rewe]].
Pitched by Jeff Johnson after a dream, from the winged goddess of victory; early buyers couldn't pronounce it, and Britons often said Nike to rhyme with bike.
The original name of the company that became [[see:Nike (company)]], founded by Bill Bowerman and Phil Knight.
An acronym of the Latin [[from:anima sana in corpore sano]], a sound mind in a sound body.
Nike's logo, designed by student Carolyn Davidson for $35; she later received Nike shares now worth millions.
Nike tagline adapted by Dan Wieden from death row inmate [[from:Gary Gilmore]]'s last words, "Let's do it."
Hans Wilsdorf wanted a short name that looked good on dials and was easy to say in any language; he said a genie whispered it in Cheapside.
From the initials S O of [[from:Standard Oil]]; still used in Britain and internationally, but replaced in the US by [[gave:Exxon]].
Many state Standard Oil companies prevented the New Jersey firm from using [[see:Esso]] nationally.
Generated by computer in 1972 as charismatic letters inspired by [[from:Esso]], with the double X echoing double S; it replaced Esso, Enco and Humble.
An American brand replaced by [[see:Exxon]].
An American oil brand replaced by [[see:Exxon]].
Named after the seashells Marcus Samuel Sr. imported from the Far East; his sons chose the name for their kerosene in homage.
Named after the giant river, chosen to start with A for alphabetical web listings and to suggest an everything store; originally [[from:Cadabra]].
Amazon's original name, short for [[from:abracadabra]], dropped because people misheard it as [[see:cadaver]].
The word that [[gave:Cadabra]], Amazon's first name.
What people misheard [[see:Cadabra]] as, prompting the name change.
A deliberate misspelling of [[from:googol]], suggesting vast information; replaced [[from:BackRub]]; now a verb, first used on [[see:Buffy the Vampire Slayer]], prompting genericization lawsuits.
Larry Page and Sergey Brin's original nickname for their search engine, because it checked backlinks to rate sites.
The number one followed by 100 zeros, coined by a mathematician's nine-year-old nephew and discussed in the maths episode; source of [[gave:Google]].
A 1919 comic strip about a gambler named Barney Google, later taken over by fan-favourite Snuffy Smith; an earlier, unrelated Google.
Enid Blyton's magical food item: a bun with a sherbet-filled currant that froths in your mouth.
Stick-on eyes for drawings, implying a word goo or google, in the same silly vein as earlier Googles.
The TV show with the first pop-culture use of [[see:Google]] as a verb.
Short for [[from:Coca-Cola]]; in the American South it can mean any soda, so asking for a Coke may get you a Pepsi.
Named from coca leaves and the [[from:cola]] nut, its first stimulants; created by John Pemberton in 1886 as an alcohol-free alternative to [[see:coca wine]].
The cola nut, chewed in West Africa as a stimulant, distinguishing [[gave:Coca-Cola]] from coca wine; later cola names refer to Coca-Cola itself.
The drink that [[see:Coca-Cola]] was made as an alcohol-free alternative to.
Where wholesome early Americans got sodas mixed, as [[see:Coca-Cola]] syrup was served with carbonated water.
Caleb Bradham's [[from:Brad's drink]], renamed Pepsi-Cola to evoke [[see:Coca-Cola]]; Pepsi probably alludes to curing [[from?:dyspepsia]] or the enzyme [[from?:pepsin]].
The original name of [[see:Pepsi]], after its inventor Caleb Bradham.
Indigestion, which [[see:Pepsi]] was supposedly a tonic for, probably behind its name.
A stomach enzyme good for digestion, another likely source of the name [[see:Pepsi]].
A brand that could be called etymologically related to [[same-root:Pepsi]].
Created by pharmacist Charles Alderton in Waco and named by Wade Morrison for unclear reasons, perhaps [[from?:pep]] or after [[from?:Charles T. Pepper]].
What soda fountain patrons in Waco, Texas, first ordered the drink as, before it became [[see:Dr Pepper]].
Energy, something that peps you up; Jess bets it lies behind [[see:Dr Pepper]] and perhaps [[see:Pepsi]].
A nostalgic British drink similar to [[see:Dr Pepper]], named after the two plants originally used to spice it.
Coca-Cola's rival to Dr Pepper, renamed from [[from:Peppo]] after Dr Pepper sued.
Original name of [[gave:Mr. Pibb]], dropped after a Dr Pepper lawsuit.
Edward Perkins's 1927 powdered version of [[from:Fruit Smack]]; a goofy spelling of cool plus -aid, probably from [[from?:lemonade]], respelled to suggest help.
Edward Perkins's liquid concentrate, dehydrated to save shipping costs, becoming [[gave:Kool-Aid]].
An old word with a French, Latin-derived ending, probably the ultimate source of the -aid in [[gave?:Kool-Aid]].
A brand from the same notion as [[see:Kool-Aid]] and [[see:Honor Maid]].
Edward Perkins's door-to-door product line, a funny spelling of honor and maid that may have started the trend leading to [[see:Kool-Aid]].
An expression with negative connotations from the Jonestown mass suicide; Kraft insists [[see:Flavor-Aid]] was used, not Kool-Aid.
A rival drink that Kraft says, rather than [[see:Kool-Aid]], was used at Jonestown.
A chaotic pitcher mascot inspired by an art director's child's smiley faces on a frosted window; he later got legs and starred in Marvel comics.
Sun-like villains fought by the [[see:Kool-Aid Man]] in Archie comics.
Once called [[see:Coca-Cola Light]] in the UK, since diet seemed too clinical; long advertised at women, unlike [[see:Coke Zero]].
The former UK name for [[see:Diet Coke]], still used in much of Europe.
Coca-Cola's sugar-free drink, marketed to men with black branding, unlike [[see:Diet Coke]].
French yoghurt brand spelled Dannon in the US so Americans wouldn't mispronounce it, as Britons do.
Americans say it like Sunday, but in England everyone says 'high and die', which Jess finds funny.
A surname, not the Roman god, naming the Anglo-American company and the British Mars bar, which is the American [[see:Milky Way]].
In the US, the bar Britons call a [[see:Mars]] bar; in Britain, a caramel-free bar closest to the American [[see:Three Musketeers]].
The American bar closest to the British [[see:Milky Way]], without caramel.
A peanut bar, once sold in Britain as [[see:Marathon]]; Rob thinks it is named after a racehorse.
The old British name for [[see:Snickers]], replaced by the international name.
Mars chocolate sold in the US, called [[see:Galaxy]] in Britain; Rob guessed it was because of Dove soap, which the US also has.
The British name for the Mars chocolate sold as [[see:Dove]] in the US.
Body spray beloved of teenage boys, spelled with an E and sold in Britain as [[see:Lynx]].
The British name for the body spray called [[see:Axe]] in the US.
The US store is called [[see:TK Maxx]] in Britain, as it could be confused with the existing shop [[see:TJ Hughes]].
The British name for [[see:TJ Maxx]], chosen to avoid confusion with [[see:TJ Hughes]].
An existing British shop whose name is why [[see:TJ Maxx]] became TK Maxx in Britain.
